podcasts.title: How To Build The Future: Paul Graham & Amjad Masad
podcasts.description: Replit was building toward the AI coding era years before it had a name. In 2024, the company shipped an agent that could take a request in plain English, work through errors, provision its own infrastructure, and keep going until the software actually worked. The model companies even reached out to ask how Replit had pulled it off.Co-founder and CEO Amjad Masad had been thinking about making programming radically more accessible since 2008, and Replit’s original pitch deck predicted AI-generated code before the Transformer paper was published. Today, that same technology is moving into banks, manufacturers, and other large companies, where Amjad says teams are replacing software projects once scoped at $10 million with $250,000 of Replit.On How to Build the Future, Paul Graham sits down with Amjad to talk about why Replit was so well positioned when coding agents arrived, what comes after vibe coding, and his bigger vision for the “self-driving company,” where AI agents increasingly build and operate the software a company needs.

podcasts.title: ⚡ Behind Latent Space: A Rare Look Inside the Pod | AIEi Shanghai
China Was Supposed to Lose the AI Race…Now Alex Karp PANICS!
podcasts.description:
China was supposed to lose the AI race. Then Palantir CEO Alex Karp started talking about whether America could stay ahead “if we’re lucky.”
Some victory lap.
In this Global Impulse reaction, we break down Karp’s revealing comments on Chinese AI, American technological dominance and why Washington’s restrictions haven’t made Chinese innovation disappear.
Karp acknowledges that Chinese engineers can work with less compute, compete on price and deliver a response he describes as “much more creative.” So much for the country that supposedly only copies.
And when the conversation turns to what “winning” means? Naturally, he brings it back to the military battlefield. Worth remembering: Palantir sells AI software to the Pentagon.
We cover:
• China’s historical influence on Japanese writing, calendars and city planning

• The schools and scientific foundations China built before Deng’s reforms

• What American pressure on Japan reveals about being Washington’s ally

• DeepSeek, model distillation and Silicon Valley’s anxiety over cheaper competition

• Palantir’s Maven military contract and Karp’s definition of “winning”

• His unexpected Tai Chi résumé detour

• Why efficient models, domestic hardware development and energy infrastructure strengthen China’s position
My money is on China. Karp doesn’t say China will win—but his own admissions make the case much more interesting than the usual American victory speech.
Does cheaper, widely available AI sound like a threat to ordinary people—or a threat to somebody’s monopoly? And what decides this race: model performance, affordable deployment or the power to run it?
Tell me in the comments. Like, subscribe to Global Impulse, and share this video with someone still calling China a copycat.

CHAPTERS

01:11 “This Was All Imported From China”
02:19 The “Copycat” That Helped Build Japan
03:31 Deng’s Embrace of Science and Industry
